where: Section 2 (Alerting and SIEM), sentence after the MTTD/MTTR definitions
problem: "Cutting MTTD does not cut MTTR" contradicts the chapter's own formula, where MTTR is measured from incident start. Since t_alert,i is inside the interval t_start,i to t_recover,i, a faster alert usually means response work starts earlier and service returns earlier, so MTTR normally falls when MTTD falls. A student will learn the opposite of what the formula shows.
fix: Replace with: "The two measure different things: MTTD stops at the alert, MTTR runs to restored service. A fast alert alone does not shorten repair, but because MTTR is counted from incident start, faster detection usually does cut downtime."

where: Worked example 1, step 2 and the answer line
problem: The example calls 30 min the "containment time", but the figure it tells students to use says containment takes 20 minutes (10 to 30 on the timeline). Two different quantities share one label, so the student cannot tell whether containment is 20 or 30 minutes.
fix: Name the quantities differently: "time to containment = 09:30 − 09:00 = 30 min", and separately "containment phase duration from the figure = 30 − 10 = 20 min". Use "time to containment" in step 2 and in the answer line.

where: Section 3, last sentence on SLA reports
problem: "A provider meeting 99.9% uptime can still have a 3-hour outage in your region" is only true if the provider measures a wider boundary than the region or a longer period. 99.9% of a 720-hour month allows about 43 minutes, so a 3-hour regional outage would breach a monthly regional SLA. Without that caveat the sentence reads as a contradiction.
fix: Add the boundary: "A provider can meet 99.9% monthly uptime measured across all regions, or over a year, and still have a 3-hour outage in your region. Read the SLA's measurement point and period before you accept the dashboard number."

problem: The text says incident response "follows six phases" as if that were the only model. The widely used NIST incident-response guide groups the same work into four phases, so a student meeting that version in another book or in an exam key will think one of them is wrong.
fix: Keep the six phases but add one line: "Some syllabi use six phases (prepare, detect, contain, eradicate, recover, learn); the NIST guide groups the same steps into four, with containment, eradication and recovery as one phase."

problem: The lead defines auditing as proving a control worked by comparing evidence with policy, and the chapter title includes auditing, but the body never explains how an audit is done — sampling evidence, testing a control, recording the result. Only the audit trail is described.
fix: Add two or three sentences in Section 1: an audit picks a control (for example, "only admins can delete buckets"), tests it against the audit trail for a period, samples entries, and records pass or fail with the evidence used.
